title: Gave and taken (Job 1:20–22)
hook: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away"

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adversary asked God about Job: does he serve for nothing? Your line was is it for nothing. Did you do one good thing nobody saw? Today, the question gets its first answer. Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

A messenger runs up to Job. Raiders came, he says, and took the oxen and the donkeys, and killed the servants, "and I only am escaped alone to tell thee." While he's still speaking, a second runs in: fire fell from the sky and burned up the sheep. While he's still speaking, a third: raiders took the camels. While he's still speaking, a fourth. Your sons and daughters were eating together in their oldest brother's house, and a great wind came from the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell on them. They're dead. The text gives us no pause between the messengers. That's the point. It all lands at once.
screen: `WHILE HE WAS YET SPEAKING.` → `ONE MESSENGER, THEN ANOTHER.` → `THE HOUSE FALLS.`

segments.voice: Now watch what Job does, in order, because the order matters. "Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped." He tears his robe. He shaves his head. He falls to the ground. Grief comes first, and it's physical, and the book doesn't hurry him past it. Jewish mourners still tear a garment at a death; the tearing is called keriah. Only then, from the ground, Job speaks: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Two things in one breath. Everything I had was given; none of it was mine to keep. And still, from the floor, a blessing. Not a blessing instead of grief. A blessing in the middle of it, with the robe already torn. The narrator adds one line: "In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly." The adversary said Job would curse God to his face. He doesn't. Tradition put Job's words into the Jewish burial service, so mourners say this line at the graveside. Some find it a comfort. Some find it almost impossible to say. Both are honest, and the book of Job has room for both: this isn't Job's last word. He'll have much more to say, and not all of it gentle. But today, this is where he stands, or rather kneels.
screen: `HE TEARS HIS ROBE AND FALLS.` · `NAKED CAME I, NAKED SHALL I RETURN.` · then, large: `THE LORD GAVE, AND THE LORD HATH TAKEN AWAY.` · then: `NOT HIS LAST WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit quietly with a loss. Settle, and breathe. Let one loss come to mind. It might be a person. It might be a home, a job, a friendship, a version of your life you thought you'd have. There's nothing to solve here, and no moral to find. Just let it sit beside you, the way Job sat on the ground. Breathe in, and notice it was given. Breathe out, and notice it was taken. You don't have to bless anything. If you pray, and if the words fit today, you can say Job's line. If they don't fit, the silence is enough. The bell holds the time.
Gave and taken. Job, on the ground in a torn robe, says what was given was never his to keep, and blesses anyway. Today's word.
Your line: gave and taken. Today, touch one thing you love, a photo, a cup, a hand, and remember that it was given. Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Jewish mourners tear a garment, called keriah, when they learn of a close relative's death, and Job's words, the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away, are part of the traditional Jewish burial service.

myth: Job blesses God before he grieves
first he tears his robe, shaves his head and falls to the ground. then he speaks.
the messengers arrive one after another, without a break
each comes while the one before is still speaking.

fork.setup: you're Job. four messengers, one after another, and the last says your children are dead. what do you do?
options: curse God, just as the adversary said you would.
tear your robe, fall to the ground, and bless the name of the LORD.
fork.reveal: he grieves with his whole body first, then from the ground says: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.

original.note: Hebrew: he gave; the verb in Job's line, the LORD gave, in Job 1:21.

trapdoor: what you thought: a calm saying about accepting loss.
what it means: a man who has just torn his robe and fallen to the ground blesses God in the middle of grief.
what a scholar hears: the adversary said Job would curse God; Job blesses instead, and the line later entered the Jewish burial service.

notes: Keriah stated as current Jewish mourning practice; please confirm wording for this path.
'Tradition put Job's words into the Jewish burial service' refers to Tzidduk ha-Din, which includes Job 1:21; please confirm.
The 'fire of God' (1:16) rendered 'fire fell from the sky'; 'Sabeans' and 'Chaldeans' rendered as 'raiders'.
'Their oldest brother's house' follows 1:18 ('their eldest brother's house').
Editor: reworded the practice's 'Don't fix it. Don't look for the lesson.', which echoed day 834's practice almost word for word.
Audit: the original-word note called נָתַן 'the first word' of the line; in Hebrew the line opens with the divine name (יְהוָה נָתַן), so it now says 'the verb'.
